topics.core_competency: The learner understands that the reaction of metals can be represented as word equations and their applications in everyday life.
learning_outcomes: understand the importance of word chemical equations (u)
read and interpret word equations (u)
understand the meaning of reactivity series (u)
use reactivity series to predict how metals react with air, water and acids.
understand how occurrence and uses of metals depend on their properties and these in turn depend on their position in the reactivity series (u, v/a)
understand what alloys are (u)
know the common alloys, their composition and their uses (k, u)
compare the properties of common metals with their alloys (u)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups and with the help of the teacher, learners: write word equations for some processes that occur in daily life
Write word equations for reactions of metals with water and dilute acids and interpret them
plan an activity to deduce the reactivity series for common metals based on their reactions with air/oxygen, water/steam and dilute acids.
Using ICT and other sources, learners search and discuss the difference in the physical properties and chemical composition of a pure metal compared to its alloy.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Engage learners in a conversation about why the more reactive metals (e.g. Groups I and II metals and aluminium) cannot be extracted by reduction with charcoal. Let learners critique the responses given by their peers.
Ask learners to compare the use of pure iron and steel in making items like knives and spoons in table form. Assess how learners translate scientific knowledge to everyday use.

suggested_uses: Using ICT and other sources, learners search and discuss the difference in the physical properties and chemical composition of a pure metal compared to its alloy.

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates that the smallest units of matter are atoms are, which are sub-divided into smaller particles and the orderliness and uniqueness of atomic structure.
learning_outcomes: understand the meaning of an atom (k)
understand the Dalton and Rutherford atomic models (k, u)
represent the structure of the atom and label the subatomic particles (k, u)
understand the meaning of mass number, atomic number, isotope and ions using standard representation (k, u)
compare atoms of different elements (u)
show by means of electronic configuration, the electron arrangement of in atoms for the first twenty elements (u, s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: use ICT and other sources to search and carry out a discussion on what an atom basing on Dalton’s and Rutherford’s atomic theory
make models of atoms using locally available materials.
In groups, learners discuss and write electronic structures of the first 20 elements

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Task learners to make atomic models for atoms with atomic number 10, 12 and 19 using locally available materials. Observe how learners select the materials and how they work together to put the materials together to get the model.

Ask groups of learners to write and draw electronic structure of the first twenty elements. Assess aspects of co-operation and leadership as learners proceed with the activity. Check that they have written the correct electron configurations.

practicals.title: Making Atomic Models
practicals.description_verbatim: make models of atoms using locally available materials.

suggested_uses: use ICT and other sources to search and carry out a discussion on what an atom basing on Dalton’s and Rutherford’s atomic theory

topic_metadata.topic_title: NATURE OF SOIL AND SOIL CONSERVATION

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates soil components and properties in relation to their contribution to life of living organisms, and the need to conserve soil.
learning_outcomes: understand what soil is and explain its importance for life on earth (u)
know the soil constituents and identify their functions (k, u)
know and state the types of soil (k)
Compare retention, drainage and capillarity in different soil samples (u)
Describe a test to find the pH of a soil sample (u)
Design experiments to find the percentage of air, water and humus in a soil sample (u, s)
know the features of a fertile soil (k)
understand the meaning of soil erosion and identify its agents and types (k, u)
assess the causes of loss of soil fertility (u, v/a)
analyse the effectiveness of the methods of soil conservation (u, s, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners search and: discuss the role of each of the soil constituents in enabling the existence of other living organisms
feel three different soil samples (clay, sand and loam) separately and record their observations based on the size and texture of particles in each soil sample

In groups, learners; feel the two types of soils provided (Clay and Sand) and transfer equal amount of each soil type to a funnel on a beaker (set-up by teacher). pour measured amounts of water onto each soil. Leave the experiment for 10 minutes. Discuss the observations.
In groups, learners discuss design simple experiment to demonstrate a chosen type of soil erosion and make a report
research and write a report on the different methods used to maintain soil fertility and to conserve soil in the following regions of Uganda: Lake Victoria basin, Kigezi highlands, Karamoja region

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Design and report on a simple experiment to show that soil is a water filter. Task learners to write the procedure for the above report, the observations and deductions made.

Ask learners to use a set of data to calculate the percentage of air and water in different soil samples. Observe how the learners substitute data in a stated formula and how they simplify the expressions to obtain the final answer.

Design a project to show that crop growth is different in different soil types. Use the following crops: Carrots, Yams (suckers), Green or chilli pepper. Assess the learners’ report for procedure, observations, deductions and any precautions

practicals.title: Soil Drainage/Retention
practicals.description_verbatim: feel the two types of soils provided (Clay and Sand) and transfer equal amount of each soil type to a funnel on a beaker (set-up by teacher). pour measured amounts of water onto each soil. Leave the experiment for 10 minutes. Discuss the observations.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: Design a project to show that crop growth is different in different soil types. Use the following crops: Carrots, Yams (suckers), Green or chilli pepper
project_requirements.deliverables_verbatim: Assess the learners’ report for procedure, observations, deductions and any precautions

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: The actual (quality) soil types should be used for experiments

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates how vital substances are recycled to maintain life.
learning_outcomes: know the sources of water as a natural resource, its physical and chemical properties and importance in everyday life (k,)
understand the role of the Sun in providing the energy to drive the water cycle and represents the water cycle diagram (u)
understand the process of water and sewage treatment (u)
apply scientific knowledge of the action of putrefying bacteria to the treatment of pit latrines (u)
understand the meaning of carbon cycle (u)
understand the role of fungi and bacteria in the decay of organic waste materials and represent the exchange of carbon within organisms diagrammatically (u)
prepare organic fertilisers for plants using recycling of plant waste (u)
understand the meaning of nitrogen cycle (k, u)
analyse processes by which nitrogen is fixed and removed from the soil (u)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups and with guidance from the teacher learners: use the listed materials to design an experiment to obtain clear water from muddy water: sand, small stones, charcoal, empty plastic bottle, course materials
design a poster of the process of sewage treatment, showing the importance of each step

In groups, learners; construct a compost container from locally available materials such as sticks, and fill it with organic waste such as banana peelings, coffee husks, tea bags, maize leaves, etc. then they leave the waste to decompose and write a report about the steps you went through
Read about the symbiotic and non-symbiotic methods of nitrogen fixation and make a report

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Design and report on a simple experiment to show that soil is a water filter. Task learners to write the procedure for the above report, the observations and deductions made.
observe learners discussing the exchange of carbon and its compounds in the environment.
Explain how nitrogen is exchanged between living things and nature. Critique the responses of the learners.

practicals.title: Water Filtration
practicals.description_verbatim: use the listed materials to design an experiment to obtain clear water from muddy water

practicals.title: Compost Container
practicals.description_verbatim: construct a compost container from locally available materials such as sticks, and fill it with organic waste such as banana peelings, coffee husks, tea bags, maize leaves, etc.
equipment_list: organic waste (banana peelings, coffee husks, tea bags, maize leaves)

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: The actual (quality) soil types should be used for experiments

topics.core_competency: The learner understands that plants are capable of making their own food from simple compounds like water and carbon dioxide.
learning_outcomes: understand the process of photosynthesis (u)
know the raw materials, conditions and products of for photosynthesis (k)
demonstrate that photosynthesis takes place in a leaf (u, s)
understand the adaptations of a leaf to carry out the process of photosynthesis (u, s)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: Internal adaptations of a leaf for photosynthesis NOT required

depth_limitations.text_verbatim: Internal adaptations of a leaf for photosynthesis NOT required

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups/pairs, learners: discuss how they would determine that photosynthesis has taken place in a leaf
feel a leaf and describe how it is adapted for photosynthesis (Broadness, thickness and veins)

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Describe the reasons for spacing crops in relation to photosynthesis.
Assess how learners relate this agricultural practice to scientific knowledge.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Internal adaptations of a leaf for photosynthesis NOT required

topics.core_competency: The learner understands the implication of their diet and plan the different diets for different categories of people.
learning_outcomes: know the meaning and purpose of nutrition (k)
identify the different food nutrients, their sources and uses to humans (k)
understand the various food deficiency symptoms (u)
analyse the concept of balanced diet in relation to age, sex and an individual’s activity (u, s, gs)
calculate body mass index (BMI) and explain its implications (u, s)
assess the dangers associated with common eating disorders (obesity, bulimia and anorexia) and use of drugs (diet pills and steroids) to change body image (u, v/a)
analyse the factors that lead to famine and hunger in some communities and suggests how famine may be minimised (u, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups/pairs, learners: design a balanced diet for one day for the following categories of people and explain why it is the most suitable: A one-year old baby, A 15-year-old boy, A pregnant mother, An eighty-year-old person
measure their weight (kgs) and height (cm) and use the results to calculate their BMI. With reference to the standard BMI chart they determine their BMI status
listen to a talk/recording on self-esteem in relation to physical differences in body shape and size.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Write a message advising the public about the negative effects of adverts pressuring people to change body shape.
Identify and explain the categories of people that are likely to be affected by famine.

practicals.title: BMI Calculation
practicals.description_verbatim: measure their weight (kgs) and height (cm) and use the results to calculate their BMI. With reference to the standard BMI chart they determine their BMI status

topics.core_competency: The learner recogonises how food goes bad and the various methods of preserving different kinds of food.
learning_outcomes: know the causes of food spoilage (k)
understand the factors that promote growth of micro-organisms on food (u)
assess the methods of preventing food spoilage in various foods e.g. milk, fish, meat, fruits, vegetables and cereals (u, v/a)
understand the principles and methods of food preservation (u)
identify the symptoms of food poisoning and devise possible ways of helping someone who has had food poisoning (u, s, gs, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups/pairs and with guidance from the teacher, learners: discuss the causes of food spoilage in a Ugandan home and how food spoilage can be prevented
discuss the traditional methods used in preserving the following types of foods and make a report: Milk, Meat, Fish, Cassava

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Outline the practices in personal and kitchen hygiene that prevent food spoilage as practiced in their homes. Let learners critique the merits and demerits of the methods outlined.
Explain how the following principles work in food preservation: Heat treatment, Cold storage, Drying

topic_metadata.topic_title: OUR BODY SYSTEMS AND THEIR FUNCTIONS I

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates that the digestive, circulatory and respiratory systems perform different functions to sustain life.
learning_outcomes: know what enzymes are and understand their properties (Details of how enzymes work NOT required) (k, u)
understand the effect of pH and temperature on enzyme activity (u)
understand the types, structures, arrangement, and functions of teeth in humans (u, s)
describes the care for teeth in humans (u, s)
understand the parts of the digestive system and heir functions (k)
understand what happens during the process of digestion and identify its products (u)
understand how the end products of digestion are absorbed and assimilated (u)
know the parts/organs that make up the human circulatory system (k)
understand the structure of the heart and how it functions (u)
compare the structure and functions of arteries, veins and capillaries (u)
know the components of blood and understand their functions (k, u)
Know the human blood groups and the importance of knowing one’s blood group in life (u)
understand the need for gas exchange in humans (u)
understand the mechanism of gas exchange in humans ( u)
understand the adaptations of the lung as an organ of gas exchange and alveolus as a surface for gas exchange (u)
analyse the variation in the percentage composition of gases in inhaled and exhaled air (u, s)
know the meaning of respiration and explain the types of tissue respiration (k)
know the importance of aerobic respiration (k)
understand the process of aerobic respiration (k, u)
understand the relationship between plants and animals in relation to respiration and photosynthesis (u)
know the word equation for anaerobic respiration in plants and animals (k)
know the products of anaerobic respiration in plants and animals (k)
identify the various applications of anaerobic respiration in everyday life (k)
understand the difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration (u)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: Details of how enzymes work NOT required
Mention the respiratory organs/surfaces for insects and the frog (No details required)

depth_limitations.text_verbatim: Details of how enzymes work NOT required
Mention the respiratory organs/surfaces for insects and the frog (No details required)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups/pairs, learners: research and discuss the nature of enzymes and write down the properties of enzymes
feel, identify and name two structural features of each type of teeth in man
basing on the observations in (ii) above, explain the adaptations of each type of tooth to its role. discuss common dental diseases and how they can be prevented.
In groups, learners identify the parts/organs that are associated with digestion of food in their bodies and highlight their roles

With guidance from the teacher, learners discuss the following scenario: Some biological washing powders contain lipase. This helps the washing powder to digest fat stains. Biological washing powders should be used in warm but not hot water. Explain why.

Learners feel the structure of different tubes representing the different blood vessels and describe the following: the thickness of the outer rim, the size of the centre hole. Then they relate the observations to veins, arteries and capillaries and suggest reasons for the differences in thickness of the blood vessels

In groups, learners: read about the roles of each parts/ organs that are involved in gas exchange (breathing). observe themselves breathing in and out and discuss what happens during this process. discuss how the human exchange gases with the environment.
Debate the following topic: “Plants and animals can live and survive entirely independent of each other” (Base your arguments on scientific facts)
In groups, learners: research the products of anaerobic respiration in plants and animals and make a report
write a design for experiments to show fermentation using yeast, and anaerobic respiration in germinating seeds
discuss and write short notes of applications of anaerobic respiration in everyday life

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners engaged in a discussion on the reasons why oral hygiene is important
Task individual learners to explain the effect of pH and temperature on enzyme activity (u)

In a conversation, task learners to suggest a reason for each of the following: the walls of the ventricles have different thicknesses, The pulse is felt in arteries only, Veins have valves. Assess how learners communicate scientifically and effectively.
Explain what takes place during inhalation and exhalation basing on the observation of their bodies. Observe how learners record what happens to their bodies during these processes.
In a conversation, ask learners to discuss what happens if the food a person eats contains more energy than one’s body needs. Allow learners to critique the responses given by the peers.
Ask individual learners to compare respiration and photosynthesis in table form. Consider how the learners organize their work and communicate.

practicals.title: Blood Vessel Models
practicals.description_verbatim: Learners feel the structure of different tubes representing the different blood vessels and describe the following: the thickness of the outer rim, the size of the centre hole

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Mention the respiratory organs/surfaces for insects and the frog (No details required)

topics.core_competency: The learner explores the nature and types of forces, how they affect objects and their uses.
learning_outcomes: identify examples of push and pull forces in everyday life and uses them to explain the meaning of force (k, u)
know examples of forces and instances where they occur (k, u)
know common examples of the effects of forces on objects (k)
Understand the terms balanced and unbalanced forces and their effects in everyday life (u)
Solve numerical problems related to the resultant of two or more linear and perpendicular forces (only) acting on a body, using simple mathematical analysis (u, s)
understand the term friction (u)
analyse the effects and uses of frictional forces in everyday life (u)
assess the factors that affect friction between two surfaces (s)
devise ways of reducing or increasing friction (u, v/a)
understand what gravity is and why it is less on the moon than on earth (k, u)
understand why objects are attracted to the earth and why the earth revolves around the sun (u)
measure weight and mass of the same object and compare them (u, s)
solve simple calculations involving the force of gravity (u, s)
appreciate the importance of force of gravity to life on earth (u, v/a)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: Treatment of F=ma not required at this point
The angle at which the resultant is inclined is not required
Only the qualitative treatment of friction is required

depth_limitations.text_verbatim: Treatment of F=ma not required at this point
Both scale drawing and mathematical (Pythagoras theorem) method can be used to obtain the resultant force of perpendicular forces.
The angle at which the resultant is inclined is not required
Only the qualitative treatment of friction is required
The use of the expression W=mg to be emphasized

suggested_learning_activities.description: As individuals or in groups, learners push a wooden block along smooth and rough horizontal surfaces into another block or a lump of plasticine and discuss the observations in relation to the effect of the force.
In groups or as individuals, learners; discuss examples of balanced and unbalanced forces from everyday life and make a report
carry out a demonstration to show the effects of balanced and unbalanced forces using a wooden block or the tag of war game
With the help of the teacher, learners: carry out experiments to investigate the factors that affect frictional force between two solid surfaces in contact
discuss the effects of friction and present a report
In groups, learners: measure weight and mass of different objects using appropriate instruments and use the results to explain the relationship between mass and weight
calculate his/her own weight on earth and what it is expected to be on the moon and compares the two values.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Using two springs, a stretched one and a compressed one, learners debate the effects of a pulling force and a pushing force. Consider how learners express themselves and how they respond to others’ responses in a peer assessment

A car got stuck on a bad road. two people tried to push it in the same direction but the car did not move. Explain. when a third person joined them to pull from the front, the car started moving. Task learners to explain why it happened like that.

Task learners to explain, in brief write up, the following observations in relation to friction: grease is applied to the moving parts of a machine. car tyres become smoother and thinner with time. it is easier to write with a pencil on paper than on glass.

The force of gravity on the moon is only about one-sixth that on earth. Learner completes the following table about a person who travels to the moon and explains, in a conversation, why the answers appear that way

practicals.title: Push/Pull Forces
practicals.description_verbatim: push a wooden block along smooth and rough horizontal surfaces into another block or a lump of plasticine

practicals.title: Balanced/Unbalanced Forces
practicals.description_verbatim: demonstration to show the effects of balanced and unbalanced forces using a wooden block or the tag of war game
equipment_list: wooden block or tag of war rope

topics.core_competency: The learner understands the relation between force, distance moved and time in relation to work, energy and power and the various sources of energy.
learning_outcomes: understand the meaning of the terms work, energy and power and states how they are related (k, u)
know the units of each of the quantities above and defines them (k, u)
identify some examples of work being done on an object in everyday life (u)
solve simple numerical problems on work done and power developed (u, s)
know energy resources with respect to Uganda (k)
understand the concept of renewable / non-renewable energy sources and their effects on the environment (u)
know the forms of energy and state the law of conservation of energy, with relevant examples (k, u)
identify everyday examples of energy transformation (u)
appreciate the various ways of energy conservation for the future (u, v/a)
understand the meaning of mechanical energy and describe instances in which potential energy is converted to kinetic energy and vice-versa (k, u)
identify the energy changes that take place in a swinging pendulum and other phenomena (u)
solve simple numerical problems involving mechanical energy (u,s)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: Derivation of P.E = mgh and KE= 1/2 mv^2 not required but only their use in calculating these energies

depth_limitations.text_verbatim: Derivation of P.E = mgh and KE= 1/2 mv^2 not required but only their use in calculating these energies

suggested_learning_activities.description: As individuals or in groups, learners: lift locks or bricks of different masses through different distances and calculate the work done in each case
use their results above to discuss the factors that determine the value of work done
lift blocks of known mass through a known distance in a given time and calculate the power developed
In groups, learners: debate the merits and demerits of the various energy resources with respect to Uganda and make a report
burn a few pieces of wood, paper or a little paraffin and discuss the challenges associated with bio-fuels
discuss methods of conserving energy for the future in relation to Uganda and make a report
In groups, learners drop a small object to the ground and identify all the energy forms that take place.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Task learners to calculate the work done and the power developed when a student lifts a weight of 800 N through a height of 10 m in 48 s. Critique how the learners identify the quantities, the formula to use, the substitution and how the final answer is stated.

Learners, in a conversation, identify the energy transformations that take place: at a waterfall, when fruit falls to the ground from a tree and when a generator is used to provide light. Allow learners to critique the responses given by their peers

Solve the problem: A brick of mass 0.5 kg falls from the top of a wall 20m high. Ignoring any friction as the brick travels through the air, calculate: the kinetic energy of the brick as it hits the ground and the velocity of the brick as it hits the ground. Critically assess how the learners follow the steps in this numerical problem, involving the use of the calculator and the substitutions they make.

practicals.title: Work and Power Calculation
practicals.description_verbatim: lift locks or bricks of different masses through different distances and calculate the work done in each case; lift blocks of known mass through a known distance in a given time and calculate the power developed

practicals.title: Bio-fuels
practicals.description_verbatim: burn a few pieces of wood, paper or a little paraffin and discuss the challenges associated with bio-fuels

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Derivation of P.E = mgh and KE= 1/2 mv^2 not required but only their use in calculating these energies

topic_metadata.topic_title: TURNING EFFECT OF FORCES, CENTRE OF GRAVITY AND STABILITY

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates how turning effect of forces is related to stability of bodies.
learning_outcomes: know daily applications of turning effect of forces (u)
investigate factors that determine turning effect (u, s)
investigate balanced and unbalanced moments, their applications and deduces the meaning of equilibrium (u)
verify the principle of moments and apply it in determining the mass/weight of rods and other objects experimentally (u, s)
Solve simple numerical problems related to balanced moments (u, s)
carry out an activity to determine the centre of gravity of a lamina of uniform and non-uniform shape (u, s)
relate the position of the centre of gravity to the stability of objects, and how this is taken into account when designing an object, e.g. a bus, a racing car etc. (u, v/a)
explore the general conditions for a body to be in mechanical equilibrium (u)

depth_limitations.text_verbatim: Examples on moments should involve one or two pivots only

suggested_learning_activities.description: As individuals or in groups, learners: balance a meter rule on a knife edge and use this observation to: Discuss the meaning of balanced moments, unbalanced moments and equilibrium; Discuss the principle of moments
raise a log at different positions from the fixed end/pivot and use this activity to determine the factors that determine turning effect

In groups, learners: cut cardboards of different irregular shapes and carry out activity to locate the centre of gravity of the cardboards. The learners then try to check for the actual centre of gravity of the cardboards by balancing

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Ask learners to find out how far from the pivot of a seesaw a student of mass 80 kg should sit in order to exactly balance a student of mass 60 kg who is sitting 2 m from the pivot. Observe how learners interpret the given data and substitute in an expression and then how they obtain the final answer.
Observe team work, leadership skills, organisational skills, and other practical skills as learners determine the mass of a metre rule using a single mass and a knife edge.

Task learners in a conversation, to explain why buses with loads in the underside boot are more stable than those where the load is in the rack at the top. Ask learners to narrate their experience in relation to loading vehicles and allow learners to critique their peers

practicals.title: Principle of Moments
practicals.description_verbatim: balance a meter rule on a knife edge and use this observation to: Discuss the meaning of balanced moments, unbalanced moments and equilibrium; Discuss the principle of moments

practicals.title: Determining Centre of Gravity
practicals.description_verbatim: cut cardboards of different irregular shapes and carry out activity to locate the centre of gravity of the cardboards. The learners then try to check for the actual centre of gravity of the cardboards by balancing

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Examples on moments should involve one or two pivots only
Variety of examples and practical activities using a metre rule are recommended

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates how simple machines are used to make work easier and their applications.
learning_outcomes: explain the term simple machines and the terminologies related to them (u)
demonstrate how simple levers, the wheel and axle, pulleys, inclined plane, gear system and screw work and state their applications (u, s)
solve simple numerical problems involving mechanical advantage, velocity ratio, efficiency and power losses of simple machines (u, s)
understand why practical machines cannot be 100% efficient and devise means of achieving a high efficiency in machines (u, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: As individuals or in groups, learners: are provided with a variety of levers such as pliers, opener, knife etc. or their pictures. Using positions of load, effort and fulcrum, learners classify the levers into 1st class levers, 2nd class levers and 3rd class levers and explain the criteria used
make an inclined plane and discuss how it simplifies raising heavy loads on a vehicle

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Learners explain the causes of power loss in simple machines and how it can be minimised. This should be done using practical examples and learners analysing themselves honestly

practicals.title: Classification of Levers
practicals.description_verbatim: Using positions of load, effort and fulcrum, learners classify the levers into 1st class levers, 2nd class levers and 3rd class levers and explain the criteria used

topics.core_competency: The learner understands the modes of heat transfer and their applications.
learning_outcomes: investigate how heat is transferred by conduction and compares the rates of conduction of heat in different solids (u, s)
assess applications of good and bad conductors (u)
understand the everyday applications of convection in liquids and air (u)
understand the causes and effects of convection currents in the atmosphere and their relation to weather/climate (u, v/a)
understand heat conduction and convection in terms of particle theory (u)
understand how heat is transferred by radiation and design an experiment to compare the radiation of heat from different surfaces (u)
identify examples of radiation of heat in everyday life and their applications (u, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: As individuals or in groups, learners: hold one end of a metallic material such as a knife in a fire flame and discuss what happens
put water in a volumetric flask and add coloured material. Then they apply a small flame at the bottom and discuss what they observe
carry out a project to compare the absorption or reflection of radiant energy by different surfaces
discuss how heat transfer is kept to a minimum in a vacuum flask.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: In a conversation, task learners to identify the examples of the applications of heat energy transfer by conduction, convection and radiation and allow for peer assessment

practicals.title: Conduction
practicals.description_verbatim: hold one end of a metallic material such as a knife in a fire flame and discuss what happens

practicals.title: Convection in Liquids
practicals.description_verbatim: put water in a volumetric flask and add coloured material. Then they apply a small flame at the bottom and discuss what they observe

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: carry out a project to compare the absorption or reflection of radiant energy by different surfaces
